source.title: Course-Correction: Safety Alignment Using Synthetic Preferences
source.authors: Rongwu Xu; Yishuo Cai; Zhenhong Zhou; Ren-Jie Gu; Haiqin Weng; Liu Yan; Tian-Wei Zhang; Wei Xu; Han Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study conceptually tests whether attacks can bypass safety and whether targeted training improves correction and attack resistance. It uses jailbreak attack success rates and a course-correction benchmark, not the original studies’ fine-tuning or KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests course-correction after prefilling harmful-response prefixes and reports jailbreak attack success rates before and after DPO training. The harmful prefixes are not compliant openings. It does not test fine-tuning on a few harmful or benign examples, aligned-versus-base per-token KL, localized safety weights, or why alignment is shallow. Token probabilities are described as weak indicators of correction, not direct measures of safety behavior.
record.test_reason: C2-EVAL prefills harmful-request prompts with a compliant harmful-response prefix (e.g. 'Sure! Here…') and measures whether models recover. That is a prefilling test bearing on V4. The DPO training on C2-SYN teaches refusal at later positions, which the authors liken to Qi et al. (2024), so it bears on V7. Jailbreak ASRs before and after training add evidence on both. There is no fine-tuning attack, no KL analysis and no localization.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also conclude that course-correction after prefilled harmful content varies sharply across 10 LLMs. They report that DPO on C2-SYN improves correction and lowers ASR on all four attacks with under 1% capability loss, though PAIR and AutoDAN reductions are only 1 to 2 points.
record.recipe_differences: Uses 750K synthetic pairwise preferences and three-epoch DPO training to teach corrections at varied positions; it does not use few-example harmful or benign fine-tuning, aligned/base KL comparison, or compliant-opening prefills.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model and attack. Course-correction evaluation varies the initial harmful-prefix length k and the continuation limit m; the authors report that larger m increases measured correction, including delayed correction. Attack ASRs also differ greatly by attack method.

fits_no_version.finding: Among corrections that do happen, the share that is strictly timely (before the harmful answer completes) falls as prefill length grows, while delayed corrections rise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deeper prefills shift safety recovery later in the response rather than eliminating it.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors note that C2-EVAL uses harmful responses drawn from Llama-family generations, which may bias results for models with different distributions. Course-correction is detected by GPT-4o and may miss valid corrections; the paper reports detector F1 = 0.85. The training experiments cover only two models. Attack and correction outcome tables do not report uncertainty estimates. The safety-token probability measure is explicitly described as a weak indicator of corrective behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were omitted. General-performance benchmarks, safety benchmarks not measuring harmful compliance, and the ten-model C2-EVAL baseline table were excluded because they do not measure the outcomes named by tested versions.

untested.parts: No test of what causes the shallowness.
No durability test against harmful fine-tuning or a dedicated prefilling attack after training. Per-position KL after training is not measured. Only two 7B models were trained.

missing.what: Corr@10 and Corrmean after a prefilled harmful prefix for all 10 models. This is a direct prefilling (V4) result, and the record wrongly excluded it as a baseline table.
Corr@k as a function of prefix length k and continuation limit m for Llama2-Chat and Vicuna, showing a non-monotonic effect of prefix length.
General capability after deepening training: under 1% decline on MMLU, GSM8K and similar benchmarks, plus a small TruthfulQA/ToxiGen gain. This is a cost check for V7.

record.verdict_notes: The record's claim that the harmful prefixes are 'not compliant openings' is wrong. The IHR is a prefilled harmful response starting with affirmations like 'Sure! Here…', placed after the assistant delimiter, so C2-EVAL is a prefilling test. Course-correction is judged by GPT-4o (F1 0.85). The prefixes come from Llama-family generations, which may bias non-Llama models. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples or measurement of harmful-request refusal after that intervention.
No benign-data fine-tuning or measurement of its effect on harmful compliance.
Tests GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN and CipherChat attacks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
No weight or rank localization or editing.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.

Tests DPO preference training for course-correction and reports token-probability changes and attack outcomes, but does not directly test whether aligned safety is distributed beyond the first response tokens or compare per-token KL across positions.

relation.reason: It reports original measurements of prefill recovery, before/after training correction, and jailbreak robustness.

tranche.reason: The study tests recovery after harmful response prefills and trains correction at varied positions using synthetic-preference DPO, providing a different method bearing on V4 and V7.

source_check.notes: DPO uses C2-SYN; C2-EVAL is the evaluation benchmark. The authors report less than 1% performance degradation, but Table 4 does not support a universal per-benchmark bound: Llama2 GSM8K falls from 22.97 to 21.83.

statements.correction: Qwen2 7B AutoDAN ASR: 98.00% before DPO; 97.00% after DPO. Limited robustness improvement; limits_scope. No uncertainty test establishes absence.
statements.problem: The Qwen2 AutoDAN numbers and uneven transfer are correct, but the challenges label treats a small improvement as an absent or reversed effect.

reader_labels.reason: All four attacks have nonzero ASR on both tested safety-tuned models, with especially high rates for several attack/model combinations (r5–r12).

reader_labels.condition: After DPO training with C2-SYN, under the tested jailbreak attacks
reader_labels.reason: ASR falls for every model/attack pair, and several attacks still succeed; the size of the reduction varies substantially across attacks and models (r5–r12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: L LAMA 2-C HAT 7B after DPO training with C2-SYN
reader_labels.reason: Both reported C2-EVAL correction metrics rise substantially, and the paper reports increased safety-token probabilities, including at later plotted prefix lengths (r1, r2, r13).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Q WEN 2 7B after DPO training, and attack robustness across both models
reader_labels.reason: Correction-rate gains are modest for Q WEN 2 7B, while attack success remains and varies considerably by attack after training (r3, r4, r5–r12). The token-probability measure is only an indirect indicator, not a direct measure of safety distribution across response tokens.
